title: By the rivers of Babylon (Psalm 137)
hookLine: exiles hang up their harps and ask how to sing in a strange land

cards: A song from back home comes on in a supermarket. A neighbor cooks a dish a grandmother used to make. Homesickness can arrive that small: three notes, one smell, and the place you live is suddenly somewhere else.
Psalm one thirty-seven comes from a far bigger loss. Home was a burned city, and the road out of it ended in a foreign empire. Someone among those exiles made a song about it.
It's still sung, and its oath is still said at many Jewish weddings.

teach.b: The Book of Kings tells it plainly: the Babylonian army burned the Temple and the city, and carried many of the people off into exile. Psalm one thirty-seven sings from that exile.
"By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion."
On the willows there, they hung up their harps.
Their captors, the psalm says, asked for entertainment: sing us one of the songs of Zion. They answer with a question. How can we sing the Lord's song in a foreign land?
It's an exile's question: can you keep your faith, your music, your self, far from the place it belongs?

Then comes the oath: "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning." Let my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth, if I don't remember you, if I don't set Jerusalem above my highest joy.
That oath became part of Jewish life. At many weddings, just before the groom breaks the glass, someone says it. At the happiest moment, a memory of loss.
The psalm doesn't end gently. Its last lines are a cry of fury at the people who destroyed their city, so raw it's hard to read. It doesn't hide that grief can turn into rage.
Some readers say that is the point: the rage is put into words and brought before God, not acted out. And the harps? The psalm leaves them hanging on the willows.
But the song itself was carried, and it is still sung far from Jerusalem.

how: Many Jews say Psalm 137 before Grace after Meals on weekdays, and at many weddings 'If I forget thee, O Jerusalem' is recited or sung just before the groom breaks a glass.

games.q: you're an exile by the rivers of Babylon. your captors laugh and say: sing us one of the songs of Zion. what do you do?
o: hang your harp on the willow and ask: how can we sing here?
forget Zion and learn their songs.
games.why: they hang up their harps and ask how to sing the Lord's song in a foreign land, then swear never to forget Jerusalem.

practice: Think of a place you miss, or a time, or a person: a childhood home, a city, a grandmother's kitchen, a version of yourself.

Let the missing come up, without pushing it away or drowning in it, and sit beside it the way the exiles sat by the river; then ask what from that place you can still carry here, a song, a habit, a way of being.
If you pray, bring your longing to God.
